bp: A paid ad-free subscription sounds like a simple bargain: the user gives the platform money, and in return the platform no longer needs to watch the user for advertising. This paper asks whether that bargain changes the data pipeline in practice. The setting is familiar large social platforms, specifically Instagram, Facebook, and X, where the ad-based business model has long made user tracking seem commercially useful. Under the GDPR, removing advertising as a purpose should matter because data collection is supposed to be tied to a stated need, kept limited to that need, and explained clearly. The paper studies the gap between three things: what the paid product seems to promise, what platform data exports show is still retained or collected, and what users believe should happen. The real object is not a model accuracy score; it is the trust boundary between a platform, a payment choice, and the private traces users leave behind.
wh: The problem is hard because data collection has more than one possible explanation. If a platform still records ad-related data after a user pays for an ad-free tier, that looks inconsistent with the idea that ads justified the collection. But platforms can answer that data also supports personalization, product improvement, safety, or other experience features. The same stored field can therefore sit inside several stories: advertising infrastructure, user preference memory, security logging, or service improvement. Users cannot inspect this directly from the product screen. They see fewer ads, but they do not see whether the underlying collection machinery changed. Legal principles such as purpose limitation, data minimization, and transparency are also harder to evaluate than a visible interface change. The paper has to compare evidence from platform exports with user expectations, because either side alone would be incomplete: exports show practice, while surveys show what people understand and normatively expect from the paid option.
naive: A smart beginner would compare the product labels. One tier has ads, one tier says ad-free, so the beginner might assume the second tier switches off ad-targeting collection and keeps only the data needed to run the service. That fails because the label describes what the user sees, not necessarily what the platform stores. Another beginner move would be to read the platform's general policy and decide whether the practice is acceptable from written claims. That also fails because broad policy language may not reveal what specific records remain in a user's export. The paper instead treats the question as an empirical privacy audit: inspect data exports and separately ask users what they expect and what they believe actually happens.
ap: The central move is to split a vague privacy promise into measurable pieces. First, the authors look at data exports from three major platforms to see whether ad-related data continues to appear under ad-free subscriptions. That turns an invisible backend practice into something that can be inspected. Second, they survey 255 Prolific participants to separate two kinds of belief. One is normative expectation: what users think should happen when they pay for ad-free service. The other is descriptive expectation: what users think platforms will actually do. This distinction matters because a skeptical user may believe platforms will keep collecting data while still thinking they ought to collect less. By comparing retained data, expected reduction, and skeptical belief, the paper identifies a mismatch rather than merely saying users are confused or platforms are unclear.
mech: The mechanism begins with one concrete comparison: ad-free versus ad-based subscription models. The paper asks whether the change in payment and advertising status is matched by a change in data collection practice. The first input is platform data exports from Instagram, Facebook, and X. These exports are treated as evidence of what the platform retains or collects about a user. The authors examine them for ad-related data that persists even when the subscription is ad-free. The output of that part is a practice-side finding: the platforms continue to retain or collect some ad-related data in ad-free subscriptions. The second input is a survey of 255 Prolific participants. The survey separates what participants think should happen from what they think actually happens. The authors then count the responses: 69 percent normatively expect data collection to be reduced, while 63 percent believe platforms would still collect about the same amount of data. The final comparison lines up three columns: observed export evidence, user privacy expectations, and user skepticism. If many users expect less collection, many also doubt platforms will provide it, and exports still show ad-related data, then the central result is a documented disconnect between visible product change, platform data practice, and user understanding.
math: The main mathematical idea is measurement under opacity. The platform's internal collection system is not directly visible to users, so the study uses observable traces as a proxy: exported records stand in for retained or collected data. The mathematical move is not a complicated formula; it is disciplined comparison. First define two groups or conditions, ad-free and ad-based service, then ask which kinds of records should differ if advertising is no longer a justification. Second, count user beliefs in a survey population. A percentage is a compact summary of repeated answers: 69 out of every 100 similar respondents, in this sample, say collection should be reduced; 63 out of every 100 believe platforms will still collect about the same amount. Third, compare expectation with practice. This is a causal-looking question, but the abstract supports it as an empirical alignment study, not proof that the subscription alone caused every retained field. The paper also uses the logic of information minimization: if a purpose disappears, the amount and type of collected information should shrink. The tradeoff is personalization versus privacy. Personalization benefits from remembering more about a user, while privacy principles ask whether each remembered detail has a necessary, transparent purpose.
dots: This paper sits with platform privacy, security measurement, and responsible web governance papers because it studies what happens at a boundary users cannot inspect. It connects to privacy work by asking what useful signal is allowed to cross from the user's behavior into the platform's long-term records, and what should stop crossing once ads are removed. It connects to information measurement because the evidence is not the platform's promise but the remaining records in data exports and the counted responses from users. It also connects to causality and policy evaluation: the question is whether changing the business model from ad-based to paid ad-free should change data practices, and whether continued collection can still be justified by another purpose such as personalization. Neighboring work on platform trust, transparency, and online harms faces the same hidden-structure problem. Users experience an interface, while the consequential decision often happens in logging, ranking, retention, or backend data use.
ww: The approach works because it avoids treating privacy as only a matter of stated policy or user feeling. Data exports give a more concrete window into practice than a product name or marketing description. They do not reveal everything, but they show records that platforms make available about a user, including whether some ad-related traces remain. The survey adds a different kind of evidence: whether the paid ad-free model carries a privacy meaning for users. The split between normative and descriptive expectations is especially useful. If users merely expected less collection and also believed platforms delivered it, the issue might be framed as possible compliance. If users merely distrusted platforms without a stated expectation, the issue might be framed as cynicism. Here the two numbers together show a sharper tension: many participants think collection should fall, and many think it probably will not. When that is paired with export evidence of continued ad-related data, the paper can argue that the mismatch is structural, not just a misunderstanding by one side.
po: The payoff is a clearer way to evaluate paid ad-free subscriptions as privacy products, not just advertising products. The paper shows that removing visible ads does not necessarily mean removing ad-related data collection or retention. It grounds that claim in exports from Instagram, Facebook, and X, and it grounds the user side in a 255-person survey. The result is useful for regulators, platform designers, and users because it points to a specific compliance pressure: if a platform keeps collecting data after the advertising purpose is removed, it must explain the purpose, minimize the data, and make the practice transparent.
limits: The abstract supports a careful empirical claim, not a complete audit of every internal database or every platform. Data exports show what is exposed through export tools, which may not equal all retained data or all backend uses. The three platforms are major examples, but they do not prove the same pattern for every ad-free service. The survey has 255 Prolific participants, so its percentages describe that sample and similar respondents, not all users everywhere. The abstract also does not prove whether each retained ad-related field violates GDPR; it raises compliance questions around purpose limitation, data minimization, and transparency.
